title: Grammar Rules 1–3
subtitle: IBPS SO / RRB SO Exam Practice
source: Bank SO IT exam-oriented question bank; reference lessons used only for topic scope.
instructions: Choose the best answer. Questions are independently authored for competitive-exam practice.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.

options.text: Each of the candidates has submitted the application.
Each of the candidates have submitted the application.
Each candidates has submitted the application.
Each of candidates have submitted the application.

questions.explanation: The distributive pronoun “each” takes a singular verb: “has”.
questions.importantPoint: Each of + plural noun → singular verb.
questions.examTrap: The plural noun “candidates” does not control the verb.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.

options.text: Every employee is required to carry an identity card.
Every employees are required to carry an identity card.
Every employee are required to carry an identity card.
Every of employee is required to carry an identity card.

questions.explanation: “Every” is followed by a singular countable noun and takes a singular verb.
questions.importantPoint: Every + singular noun + singular verb.
questions.examTrap: Do not use a plural noun immediately after “every”.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.

options.text: Both the proposals are technically feasible.
Both the proposal is technically feasible.
Both the proposals is technically feasible.
Both of proposal are technically feasible.

questions.explanation: “Both” refers to two entities and takes a plural noun and plural verb.
questions.importantPoint: Both + plural noun + plural verb.
questions.examTrap: “Both” does not take a singular verb when it is the subject.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.

options.text: Both of the applicants were shortlisted.
Both of the applicant was shortlisted.
Both of applicants was shortlisted.
Both applicants was shortlisted.

questions.explanation: “Both of the applicants” is a correct plural construction and takes “were”.
questions.importantPoint: Both of + plural noun → plural verb.
questions.examTrap: The noun after “of” must be plural in this construction.
questions.hint: Check the noun and verb together.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: The manager spoke to Ravi and me.
The manager spoke to Ravi and I.
The manager spoke to Ravi and myself.
The manager spoke to Ravi and mine.

questions.explanation: After the preposition “to”, the objective pronoun “me” is required.
questions.importantPoint: Object after a preposition: me, him, her, us, them.
questions.examTrap: “I” is a subject form, not the object of “to”.
questions.hint: Remove “Ravi and” and test the pronoun.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Whom did you invite to the meeting?
Who did you invite to the meeting?
Whom invited you to the meeting?
Who did you invited to the meeting?

questions.explanation: “Whom” is used as the object of the verb “invite”.
questions.importantPoint: Who = subject; whom = object in formal usage.
questions.examTrap: Do not choose “who” merely because it is more common in speech.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Who is responsible for preparing the report?
Whom is responsible for preparing the report?
Who are responsible for preparing the report?
Whom are responsible for preparing the report?

questions.explanation: “Who” is the subject of “is responsible”.
questions.importantPoint: Who functions as subject here.
questions.examTrap: “Whom” is objective case and cannot be the subject in this sentence.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: To whom did the officer address the letter?
To who did the officer address the letter?
Whom did the officer addressed the letter?
Who did the officer address to the letter?

questions.explanation: After the preposition “to”, the formal objective form “whom” is used.
questions.importantPoint: Preposition + whom in formal grammar.
questions.examTrap: The verb after “did” must remain in base form.
questions.hint: Check both the preposition and verb form.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Neither of the two answers is correct.
Neither of the two answers are correct.
Neither of the two answer is correct.
Neither of two answers are correct.

questions.explanation: “Neither” is singular in standard formal usage and takes “is”.
questions.importantPoint: Neither of + plural noun → singular verb.
questions.examTrap: The plural noun after “of” does not make the verb plural.
questions.hint: Identify the head word of the subject.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Either of the routes is acceptable.
Either of the routes are acceptable.
Either of the route are acceptable.
Either routes is acceptable.

questions.explanation: “Either” is singular and takes “is” in this construction.
questions.importantPoint: Either of + plural noun → singular verb.
questions.examTrap: Do not let the nearby plural noun control the verb.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: One of the applicants has cleared the test.
One of the applicants have cleared the test.
One of the applicant has cleared the test.
One of applicants have cleared the test.

questions.explanation: The head word is “one”, so the verb is singular.
questions.importantPoint: One of + plural noun → singular verb.
questions.examTrap: The plural noun “applicants” does not control agreement.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: A number of students have registered for the course.
A number of students has registered for the course.
A number of student have registered for the course.
A number students has registered for the course.

questions.explanation: “A number of” means several and takes a plural noun and plural verb.
questions.importantPoint: A number of + plural noun → plural verb.
questions.examTrap: Do not confuse it with “the number of”.
questions.hint: Compare “a number of” with “the number of”.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: The number of students has increased this year.
The number of students have increased this year.
The number of student have increased this year.
The numbers of students has increased this year.

questions.explanation: “The number” is singular and therefore takes “has”.
questions.importantPoint: The number of + plural noun → singular verb.
questions.examTrap: This is different from “a number of”.
questions.hint: Identify whether the phrase begins with “the number”.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Each boy and each girl was given a certificate.
Each boy and each girl were given a certificate.
Each boy and each girl have given a certificate.
Each boy and each girl are given a certificate.

questions.explanation: When “each” individually modifies the two subjects, the construction takes singular agreement.
questions.importantPoint: Each + singular subject → singular agreement.
questions.examTrap: Do not automatically use a plural verb because there are two noun phrases.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Every one of the machines is operational.
Every one of the machines are operational.
Every one of the machine are operational.
Every one machines is operational.

questions.explanation: “Every one” is singular and takes “is”.
questions.importantPoint: Every one of + plural noun → singular verb.
questions.examTrap: “Every one” is not the same as “everyone” in meaning or grammar.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Everyone in the department has completed the training.
Everyone in the department have completed the training.
Everyone in department have completed training.
Everyone in the departments has complete the training.

questions.explanation: “Everyone” is an indefinite pronoun that takes a singular verb.
questions.importantPoint: Everyone → singular verb.
questions.examTrap: The meaning may refer to many people, but grammatical number is singular.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Both of them are ready for the interview.
Both of them is ready for the interview.
Both of they are ready for the interview.
Both them are ready for the interview.

questions.explanation: “Both of them” is the correct plural construction.
questions.importantPoint: Both of + object pronoun.
questions.examTrap: “They” cannot follow “of” in this construction.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: It was he who prepared the report.
It was him who prepared the report.
It was he whom prepared the report.
It was him which prepared the report.

questions.explanation: In formal traditional grammar, the complement after “It was” is “he”, and “who” is the subject of “prepared”.
questions.importantPoint: Formal exam grammar may require subject-form pronouns after linking verbs.
questions.examTrap: “Whom” cannot be the subject of “prepared”.
questions.hint: Check the role of “who” in the relative clause.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Whoever completes the task first will receive the certificate.
Whomever completes the task first will receive the certificate.
Whoever complete the task first will receive the certificate.
Whomsoever completes the task first will receive the certificate.

questions.explanation: “Whoever” is the subject of “completes” and therefore is appropriate.
questions.importantPoint: Whoever can function as a subject; whomever is objective.
questions.examTrap: Do not choose “whomever” merely because the sentence is formal.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: The candidate whom the panel selected accepted the offer.
The candidate who the panel selected accepted the offer.
The candidate whom selected the panel accepted the offer.
The candidate who the panel selected accepted the offers.

questions.explanation: “Whom” is the object of “selected”: the panel selected whom.
questions.importantPoint: Relative pronoun as object → whom in formal usage.
questions.examTrap: “Who” is common in informal usage, but exam grammar may test formal case.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: The officer who approved the request is on leave.
The officer whom approved the request is on leave.
The officer who the request approved is on leave.
The officer whom the request approved is on leave.

questions.explanation: “Who” is the subject of “approved”: the officer approved the request.
questions.importantPoint: Relative pronoun as subject → who.
questions.examTrap: Do not use “whom” when the pronoun performs the action.

questions.question: Identify the grammatically correct sentence.

options.text: Each of the files has been reviewed carefully.
Each of the files have been reviewed carefully.
Each of the file has been reviewed carefully.
Each files have been reviewed carefully.

questions.explanation: “Each” is singular and takes “has”; “files” is plural after “of”.
questions.importantPoint: Each of + plural noun → singular verb.
questions.examTrap: Do not make the verb agree with “files”.
questions.hint: Find the head word of the subject.

questions.question: Identify the grammatically correct sentence.

options.text: Every student and every teacher was informed.
Every student and every teacher were informed.
Every students and every teacher was informed.
Every student and every teacher have informed.

questions.explanation: Each singular subject introduced by “every” supports singular agreement in this coordinated construction.
questions.importantPoint: Every + singular noun.
questions.examTrap: The presence of two subjects does not automatically require “were” here.
questions.hint: Look at the form after each “every”.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Neither the manager nor the assistants were available.
Neither the manager nor the assistants was available.
Neither the manager nor the assistants is available.
Neither the manager nor the assistants has available.

questions.explanation: With “neither...nor”, the verb commonly agrees with the nearer subject; “assistants” is plural, so “were” is appropriate.
questions.importantPoint: Neither...nor → verb agreement follows the nearer subject in standard usage.
questions.examTrap: Do not automatically make the verb singular because of “neither”.
questions.hint: Check the subject nearest to the verb.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Neither the assistants nor the manager was available.
Neither the assistants nor the manager were available.
Neither the assistants nor the manager are available.
Neither assistants nor manager have available.

questions.explanation: The nearer subject is singular “manager”, so “was” is appropriate.
questions.importantPoint: Neither...nor → agreement with the nearer subject.
questions.examTrap: Changing subject order can change the verb form.
questions.hint: Look at the noun closest to the verb.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Either the manager or the assistants are responsible.
Either the manager or the assistants is responsible.
Either the manager or the assistants was responsible.
Either manager or assistants has responsible.

questions.explanation: With “either...or”, the verb agrees with the nearer subject “assistants”.
questions.importantPoint: Either...or → agreement with the nearer subject.
questions.examTrap: Do not always use singular agreement after “either”.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Either the assistants or the manager is responsible.
Either the assistants or the manager are responsible.
Either the assistants or the manager have responsible.
Either assistants or manager were responsible.

questions.explanation: The nearer subject is singular “manager”, so “is” is appropriate.
questions.importantPoint: Either...or → nearer-subject agreement.
questions.examTrap: Subject order matters for agreement.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: The quality of these products is excellent.
The quality of these products are excellent.
The qualities of these products is excellent.
The quality these products are excellent.

questions.explanation: The head noun is singular “quality”, so the verb is “is”.
questions.importantPoint: Prepositional phrases do not change the number of the head noun.
questions.examTrap: Do not make the verb agree with the plural noun “products”.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: The list of shortlisted candidates is on the desk.
The list of shortlisted candidates are on the desk.
The lists of shortlisted candidates is on the desk.
The list shortlisted candidates are on the desk.

questions.explanation: The head noun “list” is singular and takes “is”.
questions.importantPoint: Head noun controls agreement.
questions.examTrap: The plural noun “candidates” is inside an “of” phrase.
questions.hint: Ignore the intervening plural noun and find the head.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: More than one candidate has qualified.
More than one candidate have qualified.
More than one candidates has qualified.
More than one candidate are qualified.

questions.explanation: “More than one” generally takes a singular noun and singular verb in standard exam grammar.
questions.importantPoint: More than one + singular noun + singular verb.
questions.examTrap: Do not treat the phrase as a normal plural expression.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Many a student has made this mistake.
Many a student have made this mistake.
Many a students has made this mistake.
Many students has made this mistake.

questions.explanation: “Many a” takes a singular noun and singular verb.
questions.importantPoint: Many a + singular noun + singular verb.
questions.examTrap: Do not use a plural noun after “many a”.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: There are several reasons for the delay.
There is several reasons for the delay.
There are a reason for the delay.
There is several reason for the delay.

questions.explanation: The real subject “several reasons” is plural, so “are” is required.
questions.importantPoint: In existential constructions, agreement follows the notional subject.
questions.examTrap: Do not let “there” determine the verb number.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: There is a problem with the server.
There are a problem with the server.
There is problems with the server.
There are problem with the server.

questions.explanation: The real subject “a problem” is singular, so “is” is required.
questions.importantPoint: There is + singular noun.
questions.examTrap: “There” itself has no number for agreement.
questions.hint: Look at the noun after the verb.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: The news is encouraging.
The news are encouraging.
The news were encouraging.
The news have encouraging.

questions.explanation: “News” is grammatically singular despite ending in “s”.
questions.importantPoint: News → singular noun.
questions.examTrap: Do not infer plural agreement from the final “s”.
questions.hint: Check whether “news” is countable in this use.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Mathematics is an important subject for the exam.
Mathematics are an important subject for the exam.
Mathematics have an important subject for the exam.
Mathematics were an important subject for the exam.

questions.explanation: “Mathematics” is singular when referring to the academic subject.
questions.importantPoint: Names of academic subjects ending in -s often take singular verbs.
questions.examTrap: The spelling does not determine grammatical number by itself.
questions.hint: Treat the subject name as one field of study.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: The police have arrested the suspect.
The police has arrested the suspect.
The police is arrested the suspect.
The police was arrested the suspect.

questions.explanation: “Police” is generally treated as a plural noun when referring to police officers collectively.
questions.importantPoint: Police → plural agreement in standard usage.
questions.examTrap: Do not use “polices” or singular agreement in this meaning.
questions.hint: Consider whether the noun refers to officers as a group.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: The committee has submitted its report.
The committee have submitted its report.
The committee has submitted their report.
The committee were submitted its report.

questions.explanation: In formal singular collective-noun usage, “committee” takes “has” and the singular possessive “its”.
questions.importantPoint: Singular collective noun → singular agreement when acting as a unit.
questions.examTrap: Do not mix singular verb with plural possessive in a formal exam sentence.
questions.hint: Treat the committee as one unit here.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: The committee have disagreed among themselves.
The committee has disagreed among themselves.
The committee have disagreed among itself.
The committee has disagreed among itself.

questions.explanation: When members act individually, a collective noun can take plural agreement in British-style usage; “themselves” supports the plural sense.
questions.importantPoint: Collective nouns may take plural agreement when members act separately.
questions.examTrap: Agreement depends on whether the group acts as a unit or individuals.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: I am one of those employees who work overtime.
I am one of those employees who works overtime.
I am one of those employee who work overtime.
I am one those employees who works overtime.

questions.explanation: The relative pronoun “who” refers to plural “employees”, so “work” is appropriate.
questions.importantPoint: Relative-pronoun agreement depends on its antecedent.
questions.examTrap: Do not automatically make “who” singular because the sentence begins with “I”.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: She is the only one of the candidates who has cleared the interview.
She is the only one of the candidates who have cleared the interview.
She is the only one of candidates who have cleared the interview.
She is only one of the candidates who has clear the interview.

questions.explanation: “Who” refers to “the only one”, which is singular, so “has” is appropriate.
questions.importantPoint: Only one of + plural noun → relative clause may take singular agreement when “who” refers to one.
questions.examTrap: Distinguish “one of” from “the only one of”.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Neither of them knows the answer.
Neither of them know the answer.
Neither them knows the answer.
Neither of they knows the answer.

questions.explanation: “Neither” is singular in formal grammar and takes “knows”; “them” is the object form after “of”.
questions.importantPoint: Neither of + object pronoun + singular verb.
questions.examTrap: Do not use “they” after “of”.
questions.hint: Check pronoun case and subject number.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Whom did the interviewer select for the final round?
Who did the interviewer selected for the final round?
Whom did the interviewer selected for the final round?
Who did the interviewer select for the final round?

questions.explanation: In formal grammar, “whom” is the object of “select”, and “did” requires the base verb “select”.
questions.importantPoint: Whom = object; did + base verb.
questions.examTrap: There are two traps: pronoun case and verb form after “did”.
questions.hint: Check both the pronoun’s role and the auxiliary.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Who did you say was responsible for the error?
Whom did you say was responsible for the error?
Who did you said was responsible for the error?
Whom did you said was responsible for the error?

questions.explanation: “Who” is the subject of “was responsible”; “did you say” correctly uses the base verb “say”.
questions.importantPoint: Case is determined by the pronoun’s role in its clause.
questions.examTrap: Do not choose “whom” simply because “did” appears earlier.
questions.hint: Find the verb that the pronoun actually controls.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: To whom should I send the revised document?
To who should I send the revised document?
To whom should I sent the revised document?
To who should I sent the revised document?

questions.explanation: “Whom” follows the preposition “to”, and “should” is followed by the base verb “send”.
questions.importantPoint: Preposition + whom; modal + base verb.
questions.examTrap: Do not use “sent” after “should”.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Both of the reports are accurate.
Both of the reports is accurate.
Both of the report are accurate.
Both reports is accurate.

questions.explanation: “Both” takes a plural noun and plural verb.
questions.importantPoint: Both → plural agreement.
questions.examTrap: The singular “is” is not compatible with the plural subject.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Every one of these documents is confidential.
Every one of these documents are confidential.
Every one these documents is confidential.
Every one of these document are confidential.

questions.explanation: “Every one” is singular and takes “is”; “documents” remains plural after “of”.
questions.importantPoint: Every one of + plural noun → singular verb.
questions.examTrap: Do not confuse “every one” with “everyone”.
questions.hint: Focus on the head phrase “every one”.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Everyone who applies must provide valid identification.
Everyone who applies must provides valid identification.
Everyone who apply must provide valid identification.
Everyone who applies must providing valid identification.

questions.explanation: “Everyone” is singular, “who applies” agrees with everyone, and modal “must” takes the base verb “provide”.
questions.importantPoint: Everyone + singular verb; modal + base verb.
questions.examTrap: There are two separate agreement/verb-form checks.
questions.hint: Check the relative clause and the modal.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: Each of the two proposals has a different risk profile.
Each of the two proposals have a different risk profile.
Each of the two proposal has a different risk profile.
Each the two proposals has a different risk profile.

questions.explanation: “Each” is singular and takes “has”; “proposals” is plural after “of”.
questions.importantPoint: Each → singular agreement.
questions.examTrap: The presence of “two” does not make “each” plural.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: The person whom I met yesterday was the branch manager.
The person who I met yesterday were the branch manager.
The person whom I meet yesterday was the branch manager.
The person who I met yesterday were branch manager.

questions.explanation: “Whom” is the object of “met”, and the main subject “person” takes singular “was”.
questions.importantPoint: Relative object → whom; singular main subject → was.
questions.examTrap: Do not let “I” determine the main verb.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: The applicants who submitted the forms on time were shortlisted.
The applicants whom submitted the forms on time were shortlisted.
The applicants who submitted the forms on time was shortlisted.
The applicant who submitted the forms on time were shortlisted.

questions.explanation: “Who” is the subject of “submitted”, and plural “applicants” takes “were”.
questions.importantPoint: Who as subject; plural antecedent → plural verb.
questions.examTrap: “Whom” would be incorrect because the pronoun performs the action.

description: Grammar application covering agreement, each/every, both, neither/either, and who/whom in exam-style questions.
